title: The Passion Narrative: The Story of Jesus’ Crucifixion and Resurrection
subtitle: The Gospel accounts, the Christian confession, and the Quranic account
summary: The four Gospels agree on the central Christian claim that Jesus was crucified and that his followers believed he rose, but they arrange and describe parts of the final days differently. Christianity makes the cross the center of salvation. The Quran honors Jesus while denying that his enemies successfully killed him and directing salvation toward faith, repentance, mercy, and worship of God alone.

seo.metaTitle: The Passion Narrative: Crucifixion and Resurrection | The Straight Path
seo.metaDescription: Jesus's final days in Christian testimony, the Quran's corrective claim, and the evidence needed for a fair decision about revelation.

sections.title: The Question at the Heart of Christian Belief
sections.body:
The Passion narratives concern more than a difference of emphasis. Christianity places Jesus's crucifixion and resurrection at the center of salvation, while the mainstream Islamic reading of the Quran denies that his enemies killed or crucified him. Both accounts cannot simply be blended into the same claim.

The Islamic invitation must face the early Christian evidence directly, then explain why the Quran is accepted as a corrective revelation. Calling it later divine knowledge is meaningful only with reasons to trust its authority. This is one of the places where the [case for the Quran](/articles/why-the-quran) is essential.

sections.title: The Christian Story in the New Testament
sections.body:
Matthew 26–28, Mark 14–16, Luke 22–24, and John 18–20 narrate Jesus’ final days. They share a broad sequence: a final meal, arrest, trial, crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, burial, and an empty tomb. Each proclaims Jesus's resurrection. Matthew, Luke, and John narrate appearances; the earliest surviving manuscripts of Mark end at 16:8 with an announcement rather than an appearance scene. Mark's later longer ending, 16:9-20, includes appearances and is received as canonical in several Christian traditions. The [USCCB notes on Mark 16](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/mark/16) explain that textual distinction. The accounts differ in chronology and detail, but all make the crucifixion and resurrection decisive.

Paul’s earlier summary in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 says Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to followers. Christian theology treats this as the heart of the apostolic proclamation.

sections.title: What Differences Can—and Cannot—Establish
sections.body:
The Gospels vary in chronology, sayings, emphasis, and the arrangement of resurrection scenes. Christians propose complementary readings; critical scholars also investigate literary dependence and theological aims. These are legitimate questions about how the narratives work.

They do not erase their shared proclamation of crucifixion and resurrection. A Muslim argument that tries to establish that no execution occurred merely from a difference in tomb details asks the evidence to do more than it can. The historical case for the central event must be assessed separately from the accuracy of every narrated detail.

[The Crucifixion and History](/articles/the-crucifixion-and-history) explains why the mainstream historical inference remains strong and where its theological interpretation requires further argument.

sections.title: Give the Christian Argument Its Full Weight
sections.body:
Christians do not usually describe the cross as God punishing an unwilling stranger. They understand Christ's saving action through their belief in his identity and willing self-giving, with different traditions explaining redemption in different ways. Paul treats resurrection as central to the Christian claim, not an optional illustration.

A Christian can therefore reasonably ask why a later text should override early testimony. That question deserves evidence about Muhammad and the Quran, not an assumption that earlier witnesses have no value. History can assess testimony about extraordinary events, even though evidence of a belief and proof of its truth remain different judgments.

Islam disputes the Christian explanation while taking the force of that question seriously.

sections.title: The Quranic Account of Jesus
sections.body:
The Quran honors Jesus as the Messiah, son of Mary, and messenger of Allah. Quran 4:157 states that his opponents did not kill or crucify him, while Quran 4:158 states that Allah raised him.

The Quran does not name another person in Jesus’ place. Classical commentators offered more than one explanation of how the event appeared to his enemies. The core Islamic belief is clear: Allah saved Jesus, raised him, and his enemies did not kill him.

sections.title: The Positive Islamic Alternative
sections.body:
Islam directs hope toward God's mercy, personal responsibility, and repentance rather than salvation through a divine Son's death. Jesus is honored as a messenger whom God raised, while worship remains directed to the Creator he served. [What Is Salvation?](/articles/what-is-salvation) explains the moral and spiritual reasoning behind that account.

This offers a coherent alternative, but coherence does not settle the historical disagreement by itself. The Islamic case needs the further judgment that the Quran has credible divine authority. [Who Is Prophet Muhammad?](/articles/who-is-prophet-muhammad) and [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran) make that judgment open to examination.

The decision is therefore not whether Jesus matters. It is which account of his mission, God's nature, and forgiveness is best supported. Love for him need not be abandoned to investigate Islam's answer.

sections.title: Follow the Question to Its Foundation
sections.body: The Christian proclamation is early and central to Christian faith. The Quran offers a real corrective claim, not a minor narrative adjustment. Islam's invitation is strongest when it faces that difference honestly, explains its account of forgiveness, and supplies reasons to trust the revelation on which the correction rests.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do the four Gospels tell one identical Passion Narrative?
A: No. They share the central story but differ in literary arrangement and individual details. Christians commonly read the accounts as complementary, while historical-critical scholars analyze the differences as evidence of each author's sources and aims.

Q: Does Islam deny Jesus?
A: No. Belief in Jesus as the Messiah and a messenger of Allah is required in Islam. The Quran affirms his virgin birth and miracles by Allah’s permission while rejecting his divinity and crucifixion.

Q: Does the Quran identify someone else who was crucified?
A: No. Quran 4:157 does not name a substitute. Muslim commentators have differed about the details, but the verse’s central claim is that Jesus was not killed or crucified by his enemies.

Q: Why does this disagreement matter?
A: The crucifixion and resurrection are central to Christian salvation theology, while Islam’s account safeguards the absolute oneness of God and Jesus’ status as His honored messenger.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
- **The Crucifixion and the Qur’an: A Study in the History of Muslim Thought**. Todd Lawson. A scholarly study of Muslim interpretations of Quran 4:157.
- **The Resurrection of Jesus: A New Historiographical Approach**. Michael R. Licona. A detailed Christian historical defense of the resurrection.
- **The Historical Figure of Jesus**. E. P. Sanders. A widely used introduction to historical study of Jesus and the early Christian movement.

quranVerses.translation: And [for] their saying, "Indeed, we have killed the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, the messenger of Allah." And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but [another] was made to resemble him to them. And indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him, for certain.

Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.
